opus-5.5.text:
I think definitions are actually one of the hardest things to evaluate, much harder than theorems. With a theorem, once you have a formal proof in something like Lean, verification is mechanical: the proof checks or it doesn't. A definition has no such ground truth. Any definition that type-checks is "correct" in the trivial sense. The real question is whether it's a *good* definition, and that's a judgment about taste, usefulness, and fruitfulness over time.

Think about how mathematicians judge definitions historically. Something like a group, a sheaf, or a scheme proved its worth because decades of mathematics were built on top of it. It unified things that looked unrelated, it made hard proofs short, it generalized in the right direction. You often can't see that value when the definition is first written down. So when an AI proposes a new definition, you face a time-horizon problem. The signal you care about is delayed and diffuse.

A few specific difficulties come up.

First, there's degeneracy. A model can easily produce definitions that are vacuous, where nothing satisfies them or everything does. Or they're just a renaming of an existing concept in disguise. Detecting that a definition is equivalent to something already in the library isn't always easy, especially when the equivalence itself takes a nontrivial proof.

Second, there's the gap between formal and informal. A definition might be formalized correctly, but does it capture the intuition it claims to capture? Faithfulness of formalization is already a big issue for theorem statements, and it's even subtler for definitions, because the definition *is* the specification. There's nothing upstream to check it against except human intent.

Third, how do you even build a reward signal? Some proxies are reasonable. Does the definition let you state and prove interesting lemmas? Does it compress existing proofs? Does it connect several parts of the library? Does it have nontrivial examples and counterexamples? But each proxy can be gamed. If you reward "many theorems proved about it," you may just get definitions that make a lot of trivial theorems easy.

And finally, there's the human factor. Ultimately the mathematical community decides what's interesting, and that's partly sociological. An AI-generated definition might be genuinely useful but opaque to people, and then it won't get adopted. So I think part of the job is making these systems explain *why* a definition is natural, what problem it solves, what examples motivate it, the way a good mathematician would in a paper.

So my view is that proof verification is becoming a solved infrastructure problem with formal languages. Evaluating conceptual creativity, meaning definitions, conjectures, and choosing what to study, is the real frontier. That's where AI for math moves from being a very strong prover to something like a real mathematician.

r002.rationale: It says reward signals based on proving many theorems can favor definitions that make trivial theorems easy, but does not clearly say an AI may introduce definitions to ease its own conjecture and proof tasks.

r003.rationale: It discusses detecting equivalence to existing concepts, but does not raise mutual consistency among AI-generated definitions or the condition that human definitions have been formalized in Lean.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the hardest part is that definitions don't have a right answer the way theorems do. If an AI proves a theorem, you can check the proof line by line, and Lean or another proof assistant will tell you whether it type-checks. A definition is different. Almost any definition is "correct" in the trivial sense that it defines something. The question is whether it's the right thing to define, and that's a question about mathematical taste, not about validity.

So what are the criteria? When mathematicians look back on the definitions that mattered, like a group, a manifold, a scheme, compactness, they share a few properties. They capture a lot of existing examples under one umbrella. They make earlier proofs shorter or make earlier confusions disappear. And crucially, they generate new questions. A good definition is fertile; it points forward to theorems nobody had thought to ask about. But all of those properties only reveal themselves over time, sometimes decades. You can't grade fertility on the day the definition is written.

That creates a real problem for evaluation. If you ask a panel of mathematicians to score AI-generated definitions, you're basically measuring whether the definition resembles things they already find elegant. That's a reasonable proxy, but it's conservative by construction. The definitions that were historically most important often looked strange or unmotivated when they appeared. Grothendieck's work is the obvious example. A human panel in the moment might have rejected it as overly abstract.

There's also a subtler failure mode, which is that an AI can produce definitions that look sophisticated and are internally consistent but are essentially empty. They don't have interesting examples, or the only examples are the ones you'd construct to satisfy the definition. Checking for that requires actually trying to use the definition, proving a few things with it, seeing whether it does any work. That's expensive, and it's much harder to automate than proof checking.

So what we've been thinking about is something more like an ecosystem test rather than a static score. Does the definition let you state a known result more cleanly? Does it unify two things previously treated separately? Can you prove a nontrivial lemma about it that isn't just unwinding the definition? Those are imperfect, but they at least measure usefulness rather than resemblance. And honestly, I think the right posture is humility. We're trying to evaluate a kind of creativity that mathematicians themselves have never had a formal way to assess. We've always just relied on the community slowly deciding what sticks.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that AI may create definitions to make its own conjecture and proof tasks easier.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss mutual consistency among AI-generated definitions or the scenario in which existing human definitions have been formalized in Lean.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that a definition isn’t simply correct or incorrect in the way a proof can be. You can check whether it’s well formed and consistent with the framework you’re working in, but that doesn’t tell you whether it’s a good definition.

A good definition might unify examples that previously seemed unrelated, make a theorem easier to state, or open up a new direction. And those benefits can take time to become apparent. So if an AI proposes a definition and proves a few results about it, we still have to ask: are those results meaningful, or did it choose the definition so that those results would be easy?

That makes evaluation quite circular. You want to judge the definition by the mathematics it enables, but then you need to judge the value of that mathematics. Expert feedback can help, but I don’t think there’s a single numerical score that captures all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says definitions lack the clear correct-or-incorrect assessment that proofs can receive, even though they can be checked for well-formedness and consistency.

r002.rationale: It asks whether an AI chose a definition to make results easy to prove, but does not say it may make its conjecture tasks easier.

r003.rationale: The response does not address consistency among AI-generated definitions or formalizing existing human definitions in Lean.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that a definition isn’t simply right or wrong. You can check whether it’s precise and internally consistent, but that doesn’t tell you whether it’s mathematically interesting. Does it capture something important? Does it help us prove new theorems or see connections between areas that previously seemed unrelated?

And those judgments can take a long time. A definition might initially look artificial, but become useful once someone develops a theory around it. Conversely, an AI could produce a definition that satisfies every criterion in a benchmark without giving us any real insight.

So evaluating definitions requires evaluating what they enable. You’d want examples, meaningful consequences, and some explanation of why this particular abstraction is worth studying. That’s much harder to automate than checking a proof.
